source: [From the Apostolic Constitution "Divinae Consortium Naturae," Aug. 15, 1971. Translated for this site from the official Latin text; vatican.va gives no English.]
text: ... Hence the proper importance of Confirmation in the sacramental initiation by which the faithful, as living members of Christ, are incorporated into him and configured to him through Baptism, Confirmation and the Eucharist. In Baptism the newly baptized receive the remission of sins, adoption as children of God and the character of Christ, by which they are joined to the Church and first become sharers in the priesthood of their Saviour (cf. 1 Pet 2:5, 9). Through the sacrament of Confirmation those who have been born again in Baptism receive the inexpressible Gift, the Holy Spirit himself, by whom they are "endowed with special strength"; and, marked with the character of this sacrament, they are "bound more perfectly to the Church" and "more strictly obliged to spread and defend the faith, as true witnesses of Christ, by word and deed together" (LG 11). Finally, Confirmation is so closely joined with the Holy Eucharist that the faithful, already marked by holy Baptism and Confirmation, are fully incorporated into the Body of Christ by sharing in the Eucharist. ...

From what we have recalled it is clear that in the rite of confirming, in East and West alike, though in different ways, the first place has been held by the anointing with chrism, which in a certain way represents the apostolic laying on of hands. Since this anointing with chrism fittingly signifies the spiritual anointing of the Holy Spirit who is given to the faithful, we wish to confirm its existence and its importance.

As for the words spoken at the anointing, we have weighed with due esteem the dignity of the venerable formula used in the Latin Church; we judge, however, that it should give way to the very ancient formula proper to the Byzantine rite, which expresses the Gift of the Holy Spirit himself and recalls the outpouring of the Spirit on the day of Pentecost (cf. Acts 2:1-4, 38). We therefore adopt this formula, rendering it almost word for word.

Therefore, so that the revision of the rite of Confirmation may fittingly extend to the essence of the sacramental rite itself, by our supreme apostolic authority we decree and establish that in the Latin Church the following is to be observed from now on: The sacrament of Confirmation is conferred through the anointing with chrism on the forehead, which is done by the laying on of the hand, and through the words: "Accipe signaculum doni Spiritus Sancti" (Receive the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit).

The laying of hands on the elect, done with the prescribed prayer before the anointing, does not belong to the essence of the sacramental rite; it is nevertheless to be held in high esteem, since it contributes to the integral perfection of the rite and to a fuller understanding of the sacrament. This laying on of hands that comes first is clearly distinct from the laying on of the hand with which the anointing with chrism is made on the forehead.

topic: The ministries of lector and acolyte
source: [From the Apostolic Letter (Motu Proprio) "Ministeria Quaedam," Aug. 15, 1972. Translated for this site from the official Latin text; vatican.va gives no English.]
text: ... Among the particular offices to be kept and adapted to present needs are those more closely connected with the ministries of the Word and of the Altar, which in the Latin Church are called the lectorate, the acolytate and the subdiaconate. It is fitting that they be kept and adapted in such a way that from now on there are two offices, that of Lector and that of Acolyte, the latter also including the functions of the Subdeacon. ...

It is in keeping with the reality itself and with the outlook of our time that the ministries spoken of above should no longer be called minor orders, and that their conferral should be called not "ordination" but "institution"; and that only those who have received the diaconate should properly be, and be held to be, clerics. In this way the difference between clerics and laity will also appear more clearly, between what is proper to and reserved for clerics and what can be entrusted to the lay faithful; and so the mutual relation will appear more plainly by which "the common priesthood of the faithful and the ministerial or hierarchical priesthood, though they differ in essence and not only in degree, are nonetheless ordered to one another; each in its own proper way shares in the one priesthood of Christ" (LG 10).
... By our apostolic authority we decree the following, departing, if and in so far as necessary, from the provisions of the Code of Canon Law in force until now, and we promulgate it by this Letter:
I. First tonsure is no longer conferred; entrance into the clerical state is joined to the diaconate.
II. What until now were called minor orders are henceforth to be called "ministries".
III. Ministries may be entrusted to lay members of the faithful, so that they are no longer considered reserved to candidates for the sacrament of Order.

IV. The ministries to be kept in the whole Latin Church, adapted to present needs, are two, that of Lector and that of Acolyte. The functions hitherto entrusted to the subdeacon are entrusted to the lector and the acolyte, and consequently the major order of the subdiaconate no longer exists in the Latin Church. Nothing prevents the acolyte from also being called subdeacon in some places, if the episcopal conference so judges. ...
VII. In accordance with the venerable tradition of the Church, institution as lector and acolyte is reserved to men. ...

source: [From the Letter to Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, Prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, April 8, 1988. Translated for this site from the official Italian text; vatican.va gives no English.]
text: ... In the post-conciliar period we have witnessed a great effort of the Church to make this "novum" constituted by Vatican II enter rightly into the consciousness and life of the individual communities of the People of God. Alongside this effort, however, tendencies have appeared that create a certain difficulty on the way to carrying out the Council. One of these tendencies is marked by a desire for changes that are not always in harmony with the teaching and spirit of Vatican II, even though they seek to appeal to the Council. These changes are meant to express progress, and so this tendency is called "progressivism". Progress, in this case, is an aspiration toward the future that breaks with the past, without taking account of the function of Tradition, which is fundamental to the Church's mission so that she may endure in the Truth handed on to her by Christ the Lord and the Apostles and diligently guarded by the Magisterium.

The opposite tendency, usually called "conservatism" or "integrism", stops at the past itself, without taking account of the rightful aspiration toward the future that showed itself precisely in the work of Vatican II. While the first tendency seems to regard as right whatever is new, the other sees what is right only in what is "old", taking it as a synonym for Tradition. Yet it is neither the "old" as such nor the "new" in itself that corresponds to the right concept of Tradition in the life of the Church. That concept means the Church's faithful abiding in the truth received from God, through the changing events of history. The Church, like the householder in the Gospel, wisely brings out "from his treasure what is new and what is old" (cf. Mt 13:52), remaining absolutely obedient to the Spirit of truth whom Christ gave the Church as her divine Guide. And the Church carries out this delicate work of discernment through the authentic Magisterium (cf. Lumen Gentium 25).

The positions taken by persons, groups or circles linked with one tendency or the other can be understood to a certain extent, especially after so important an event in the history of the Church as the last Council. If on the one hand it released an aspiration to renewal (and this contains an element of "newness"), on the other hand certain abuses on the way of this aspiration, in so far as they forget the essential values of Catholic doctrine on faith and morals and in other areas of the Church's life, for example the liturgical, can and indeed must provoke a just objection. If, however, because of such excesses every sound "renewal" in keeping with the teaching and spirit of the Council is rejected, then such an attitude can lead to another deviation, which is equally contrary to the principle of the living Tradition of the Church, obedient to the Spirit of truth. ...

source: [From the Address to the Plenary Session of the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, Oct. 31, 1992. Translated for this site from the official French text; vatican.va gives no English.]
text: ... If contemporary culture is marked by a tendency to scientism, the cultural horizon of Galileo's age was unified and bore the imprint of a particular philosophical formation. This unified character of culture, which is in itself positive and desirable even today, was one of the causes of Galileo's condemnation. The majority of theologians did not perceive the formal distinction between Sacred Scripture and its interpretation, and this led them to carry over unduly into the field of the doctrine of the faith a question of fact that belonged to scientific investigation. ...

Cardinal Poupard has also reminded us how the sentence of 1633 was not irreformable, and how the debate, which had never ceased to develop, was closed in 1820 with the imprimatur granted to the work of Canon Settele. ...

From the Galileo affair one can draw a lesson that remains relevant to similar situations that arise today and may arise tomorrow. In Galileo's time it was inconceivable to picture a world without an absolute physical point of reference. And since the cosmos then known was, so to speak, contained within the solar system alone, that point of reference could be placed only on the earth or on the sun. Today, after Einstein and in the perspective of contemporary cosmology, neither of these two points of reference has the importance it had then. This remark does not, of course, bear on the validity of Galileo's position in the debate; it means to show that often, beyond two partial and contrasting views, there is a wider view that includes and surpasses them both.

Another lesson is that the various disciplines of knowledge call for a diversity of methods. Galileo, who practically invented the experimental method, had understood, thanks to his intuition as a physicist of genius and relying on various arguments, why only the sun could function as the centre of the world as it was then known, that is, as a planetary system. The error of the theologians of the time, when they upheld the centrality of the earth, was to think that our knowledge of the structure of the physical world was in some way imposed by the literal sense of Sacred Scripture. Let us recall the celebrated saying attributed to Baronius: "Spiritui Sancto mentem fuisse nos docere quomodo ad coelum eatur, non quomodo coelum gradiatur" (the Holy Spirit meant to teach us how one goes to heaven, not how the heavens go). In reality, Scripture does not concern itself with the details of the physical world, the knowledge of which is entrusted to human experience and reasoning. There are two realms of knowledge: one that has its source in Revelation, and one that reason can discover by its own powers. To the latter belong in particular the experimental sciences and philosophy. The distinction between the two realms of knowledge should not be understood as an opposition. The two realms are not altogether external to each other; they have points of meeting. The methods proper to each make it possible to bring out different aspects of reality. ...

For humanity there is a twofold mode of development. The first comprises culture and scientific and technical research, that is, everything that belongs to the horizontal dimension of man and of creation, and it is growing at an impressive pace. If this development is not to remain wholly external to man, it presupposes a corresponding deepening of conscience and its exercise. The second mode of development concerns what is deepest in the human being when, transcending the world and transcending himself, man turns to the One who is the Creator of all things. Only this vertical movement can, in the end, give full meaning to man's being and acting, for it places him between his origin and his end. In this twofold movement, horizontal and vertical, man fully realizes himself as a spiritual being and as homo sapiens. But one observes that development is neither uniform nor in a straight line, and that progress is not always harmonious. This shows the disorder that affects the human condition. The scientist who becomes aware of this twofold development and takes it into account contributes to the restoration of harmony.

Whoever undertakes scientific and technical research presupposes that the world is not a chaos but a "cosmos", that is, that there is an order and natural laws which can be grasped and thought, and which therefore have a certain affinity with the mind. Einstein liked to say: "What is eternally incomprehensible about the world is that it is comprehensible." This intelligibility, attested by the astonishing discoveries of the sciences and of technology, points in the end to the transcendent and primordial Thought whose imprint all things bear.

topic: The origin of life and evolution
source: [From the Message to the Plenary Assembly of the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, Oct. 22, 1996. Translated for this site from the official French text; vatican.va gives no English.]
text: ... In his encyclical Humani Generis (1950), my predecessor Pius XII had already affirmed that there was no opposition between evolution and the doctrine of the faith about man and his vocation, provided that one did not lose sight of certain fixed points (cf. n. 2327).

For my part, when I received the participants in the plenary assembly of your Academy on 31 October 1992, I had occasion, in connection with Galileo, to draw attention to the need for a rigorous hermeneutic for the correct interpretation of the inspired word. The proper sense of Scripture must be carefully delimited, setting aside undue interpretations that make it say what it does not intend to say. To mark out clearly the field of their own object, the exegete and the theologian must keep themselves informed of the results to which the natural sciences lead.

Taking into account the state of scientific research at the time, and also the proper requirements of theology, the encyclical Humani Generis considered the doctrine of "evolutionism" a serious hypothesis, worthy of investigation and reflection as thorough as that given to the opposite hypothesis. Pius XII added two conditions of method: that this opinion not be adopted as if it were a certain and demonstrated doctrine, and as if one could set Revelation entirely aside with regard to the questions it raises. He also stated the condition on which this opinion was compatible with the Christian faith, a point to which I shall return.

Today, almost half a century after the encyclical appeared, new knowledge leads to the recognition that the theory of evolution is more than a hypothesis. It is indeed remarkable that this theory has progressively won the acceptance of researchers, following a series of discoveries made in various fields of knowledge. The convergence, neither sought nor contrived, of the results of studies carried out independently of one another is in itself a significant argument in favour of the theory.

What is the significance of such a theory? To take up this question is to enter the field of epistemology. A theory is a meta-scientific elaboration, distinct from the results of observation but consistent with them. By means of it a set of data and facts independent of one another can be linked and interpreted in a single explanation. A theory proves its validity to the extent that it can be verified; it is constantly measured against the facts; where it ceases to be able to account for them, it shows its limits and its inadequacy, and must be rethought.
Moreover, the elaboration of a theory such as that of evolution, while obeying the requirement of consistency with the data of observation, borrows certain notions from the philosophy of nature.

And to tell the truth, rather than of the theory of evolution one should speak of the theories of evolution. This plurality arises on the one hand from the diversity of the explanations proposed for the mechanism of evolution, and on the other from the various philosophies to which they refer. There are thus materialist and reductionist readings, and spiritualist readings. The judgment here belongs properly to philosophy and, beyond it, to theology.

The Magisterium of the Church is directly concerned with the question of evolution, for it touches the conception of man, of whom Revelation teaches that he was created in the image and likeness of God. The conciliar constitution Gaudium et Spes has set out this doctrine magnificently; it is one of the axes of Christian thought. It recalled that man is "the only creature on earth that God has willed for its own sake" (GS 24). In other words, the human individual cannot be subordinated as a mere means or a mere instrument either to the species or to society; he has value for his own sake. He is a person. By his intellect and his will he is capable of entering into a relationship of communion, solidarity and self-giving with his fellows. Saint Thomas observes that man's likeness to God lies especially in his speculative intellect, because his relation to the object of his knowledge resembles God's relation to his work. But more still, man is called to enter into a relationship of knowledge and love with God himself, a relationship that will find its full flowering beyond time, in eternity. In the mystery of the risen Christ the whole depth and greatness of this vocation are revealed to us. It is by virtue of the spiritual soul that the whole person, even in the body, possesses such dignity. Pius XII had stressed this essential point: if the human body takes its origin from pre-existing living matter, the spiritual soul is immediately created by God ("animas enim a Deo immediate creari catholica fides nos retinere iubet").

Consequently, theories of evolution which, according to the philosophies that inspire them, regard the spirit as emerging from the forces of living matter or as a mere epiphenomenon of that matter are incompatible with the truth about man. They are, moreover, incapable of grounding the dignity of the person.

With man, then, we find ourselves before a difference of an ontological order, before an ontological leap, one might say. But does not positing such an ontological discontinuity run counter to the physical continuity that seems to be the guiding thread of research on evolution, from the level of physics and chemistry onward? Consideration of the method used in the different orders of knowledge makes it possible to reconcile two points of view that would seem irreconcilable. The sciences of observation describe and measure with ever greater precision the many manifestations of life and place them on the line of time. The moment of passage to the spiritual is not the object of observation of this kind, which can nevertheless discover, at the experimental level, a series of very valuable signs of what is specific to the human being. But the experience of metaphysical knowledge, of self-awareness and reflection, of moral conscience, of freedom, or again aesthetic and religious experience, belong to philosophical analysis and reflection, while theology brings out their ultimate meaning according to the Creator's plans. ...
